pronunciation.approximation: KYOO-shoo, with the compressed ky- onset and long vowels.
pronunciation.note: Kyūshū 九州 — "Nine Provinces" — carries the long ū in both syllables, both preserved in the restoration. The name remembers the island's ancient division into nine provinces; its older name, Tsukushi, appears in the earliest chronicles as the gateway of the gods' descent. Both syllables are long in kana (きゅうしゅう); the two macrons of the restoration are the two doubled vowels.

domains.title: The Nine Provinces
domains.subtitle: The Gateway, the Kamikaze, and the Christian Century
domains.lead: Kyūshū is Japan's front door: the island facing Korea and China across the narrowest straits, where the continent's rice, Buddhism, and iron first arrived — and where the Mongol fleets, the Portuguese traders, and the Jesuit fathers all made their landfall. The gateway of Japan has always stood open on this shore, even when the country tried to shut it.

cards.name: The Straits
cards.desc: Tsushima and Korea are a day's sail — Asia has always been closer here than Tōkyō.

cards.name: The Kamikaze
cards.desc: The "divine wind" typhoons of 1274 and 1281 that shattered two Mongol invasion fleets off this coast.

cards.name: Nagasaki
cards.desc: The one window kept open in the closed country: two centuries of Dutch and Chinese trade through a single fan-shaped island.

mythology.lead: Kyūshū claims the mythology of beginnings: the chronicles land the sun goddess's grandson on its peaks, and its storms wrote themselves into the national soul.

myths.title: Ninigi on Takachiho
myths.text: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki bring the heavenly grandson Ninigi down to earth on the peak of Takachiho — placed by tradition in Kyūshū's mountains — where he marries the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime. She proves her divine conception by setting fire to the birthing hut and delivering three sons amid the flames; their line leads to Jimmu, the first emperor. The imperial charter myth is, geographically, a Kyūshū story.

myths.title: The Divine Wind
myths.text: Twice the Mongol-Chinese fleets of Kublai Khan reached Kyūshū — 1274 and 1281, the second numbering thousands of ships — and twice, after hard fighting on the Hakata beaches, typhoons destroyed the armadas. The shrines had prayed for deliverance, and the nation named the storm kamikaze, "divine wind": weather as providence, and the coast of Hakata Bay as the sacrificial altar of the world's largest seaborne invasions.

myths.title: The Kirishitan Century
myths.text: Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549; within decades Kyūshū had a quarter-million Christians, daimyō baptized with their domains, and seminaries at Arima and Azuchi. Then came the turn: persecution, crucifixions at Nagasaki, the Shimabara-Amakusa rising of 1637 — and 250 years of hidden Christians keeping Latin prayers in corrupted Japanese, baptizing in secret, venerating statues of Kannon as Maria. Their revelation in 1865, when farmers of Urakami knelt before a French priest, stunned the mission world.

lore.syncretism: Kyūshū is Japan's syncretic laboratory: Korean potters founding Arita porcelain, Chinese merchant quarters at Nagasaki, Portuguese words entering the language (pan, tempura, kappa), Dutch learning (Rangaku) flowing through Dejima into Japanese science — anatomy, astronomy, and artillery smuggled in translation. The island's cuisine, dialects, and crafts all carry the gateway's mark: everything Japanese that came from outside came here first.
lore.culturalLegacy: The kamikaze of 1281 gave the 20th century its most terrible word; Nagasaki's 1945 atomic bombing made the island a symbol of the nuclear age's cost, and its peace park one of the world's pilgrimage sites of memory. Arita and Imari porcelain conquered European markets and imitators for three centuries. Today the island's universities and semiconductor fabs continue the oldest pattern: the gateway as Japan's technology shore.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Kyūshū is the island that opens. Rice, writing, Buddhism, gunpowder, Christianity, Western science — all knocked on this shore, and Japan answered differently each time: embrace, storm, secrecy, translation. It asks the gateway's question, which is every border's question: what do you let in — and what does the letting-in make of you?

The gateway's pattern persists in silicon: the island that took in rice, iron, scripture, and surgery now takes in the semiconductor supply chain, and Kumamoto's fabs are Tsukushi's old role in new matter. Every borderland knows its double exposure — first to the gift, first to the invasion — and Kyūshū's answer has been constant for two thousand years: translate everything, fear nothing twice, and keep the door's hinges oiled.

And the island's two great memories — the divine wind and the atomic one — face each other across eight centuries: the storm that saved and the bomb that burned, both arriving from the same sky over the same coast. Kyūshū carries them without resolving them, which is the gateway's last lesson: the shore that opens to the world must be ready for everything the world brings, the sutra and the cannonball, the virus and the vaccine, the answer arriving, as always, by sea.

The straits have not moved; the gateway still opens each morning to the same west. What changes is only the cargo — sutras once, silicon now — and the island's ancient readiness to receive it, translate it, and make it Japanese.
lore.archaeology: Yoshinogari, in Saga, is East Asia's great Yayoi site: a moated, towered settlement of two thousand years ago, with mass jar-burials and bronze-weapon caches — the archaeological face of the Wa people whom Chinese chronicles describe. The underwater archaeology of Takashima's Mongol wrecks — anchor stones, bombs, and hulls preserved in Imari Bay — has recovered the kamikaze fleets themselves. The hidden Christian sites of the Amakusa islands and Nagasaki's Ōura Cathedral (1864, built for the returned faith) are UNESCO-listed as the "Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region."
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 九州: kyū (nine) plus shū (province). The island's ancient name 筑紫 (Tsukushi) is preserved in the Kojiki's island-birth account — "Kyūshū" is the administrative name that replaced the mythic one and quietly kept the older island's memory of division.
